references.text: God created man in his image (tselem) and likeness (demut). In Gen 5:3 the same words are used to describe that Adam had a son in his likeness and image, showing the continuation of God's image through generations.
Adam again had relations with his wife, and she bore a son and named him Seth. This is the parallel account of Seth's birth, described in Gen 5:3 as Adam having a son in his own likeness and image.
On the day God created man, he created him in God's likeness (demut). This is the immediate context for verse 5:3, where Adam similarly has a son in his own likeness and image.
Whoever sheds human blood, by humans shall their blood be shed, for in God's image he made mankind. The verse confirms that God's image (tselem) in humanity continues, as also expressed in Gen 5:3.

Paul contrasts the first Adam, who became a living soul, with the last Adam (Christ), who became a life-giving spirit. The earthly image of Adam (v. 49) is linked to the heavenly image, building on the image theme from Gen 5:3.
Luke's genealogy ends with "Adam, son of God," reflecting the relationship in Gen 5:3 where Adam has a son in his image, just as Adam himself was created in God's image.
